title: SEC Proposes First Major Transfer-Agent Rule Update Since 1980s, Explicitly Embracing Blockchain (September 1, 2026)
dek: The SEC proposed on September 1 to modernize transfer-agent rules unchanged since the late 1970s and early 1980s. The proposal explicitly permits electronic communications and blockchain technology in securities offerings and share transfers. Public comment runs for 60 days after Federal Register publication.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: Transfer-agent rules have not been substantively updated in over 40 years; the SEC's first major modernization explicitly names blockchain as an authorized mechanism for securities transfer.
bottom_line: The 60-day comment period beginning after Federal Register publication is the next procedural milestone; observers should monitor whether the final rule carries limiting language on blockchain use or establishes new custody standards that would constrain on-chain settlement infrastructure.
body: The SEC proposed on September 1 to modernize transfer-agent rules that have not been substantively updated since the late 1970s and early 1980s. The modernization explicitly permits transfer agents to use electronic communications and blockchain technology in connection with securities offerings and the transfer of shares, per the SEC's press release.

Transfer agents are a key component of the U.S. national clearance and settlement system. The current ruleset predates widespread electronic recordkeeping and digital asset markets, leaving the regulatory framework misaligned with how transfer agents operate today.

The SEC's proposal would amend existing rules and forms, rescind one rule, and introduce new rules that apply to registered transfer agents and their activities. According to the SEC, the updated rules would streamline and modernize the framework to reflect transfer agents' current processes and operations, as well as the technological environment in which they function.

The public comment period will remain open for 60 days after the date of publication in the Federal Register. The SEC's press release does not identify which existing rules will be rescinded or what specific new rules the agency intends to introduce.

The modernization represents the first comprehensive update to transfer-agent rules in over four decades. The explicit inclusion of blockchain technology in the proposal marks a direct regulatory acknowledgment that electronic and distributed-ledger systems are operational features of U.S. securities markets, not experimental parallel structures.
